19.history: The town of the Red Hill, fifty-five miles west of Dùn ìseal, had its bridge thrown by Ailean Clachair's fellowship and widened in Mòrag nan Rathad's time. It became the seat of the island in FE 1,699, when Beathag Mhòr moved the hall from Dùn dhearg to the plain, and it was called the red hall from then on. Beathag Mhòr ordered the census of hands from here. The red hall's clerks kept the king-list in six copies and a roll that outgrew its room. A stable-boy's fisher-tally scratched on a granary door taught a clerk's daughter her letters. Lachlann Bàn and Raonaid Dhubh made the shared-meal law here. After Oighrig nic Lachlainn's death the hall stood shut, and then Gilleasbuig Mòr slept in its clerks' room for five-and-twenty years. Anna Ruadh set out from it on foot twice. Coinneach Bàn had every province's laws copied into its chests. Mòr nic Coinnich died here, and her daughter Beathag was crowned here without going to Dùn ìseal.
19.known_for: the red hall and its rolls

204.history: The lords of the western plain founded the market town, and in the seventeenth century they made the fleece of a grown ewe its measure. Grain, wine, cattle and the horses of the plain were priced in fleeces; the silver rings of Muileann chiar were taken there too, but reckoned in wool. Beathag Mhòr came to its fleece-market as a young queen and rode home by the northern road, and found a waypoint house there thin-fed and sent it grain.

391.history: Millers of the central country founded the town twenty-seven miles west of the Hall. After the Silver Feud, Beitris nic Aonghais cast the first bronze copy of the Muileann chiar weight here in FE 1,751. It cracked along its rim from cooling too fast, and she kept it all her life to show her apprentices. She asked leave to cut Sliochd Fhearchair's hearth-sign under every copy, and it was granted. Her family of casters went on to cast bells, pins and lamp-bowls, and their lamp-bowls held the Law's measure exactly.
391.known_for: the bronze weights and the lamp-bowls

62.history: Boat-builders of the north-east founded the town on the Abhainn bheag. In the eighteenth century a teacher of the stag's people, once a cutter's son, settled here and taught fisher-marks to children who would never cut coal. It was the first teaching of letters for their own sake, and the Hall's roll noted that fish do not need to read. He taught three generations of the same dozen families, and when he died a pupil cut his grave-marker in the fisher-marks, the first stone on the island so cut. A boy of Inis bheag, sent to the red hall's stables, carried the marks inland.

132.history: The old harbour of the Seann-Dhaoine on the northern coast was the home of the fowler families, who fed their hawks before the household ate and burned their season's handful at dawn with the hawk on the wrist, since the flame, they said, is a hunger and should be fed as a hunger is. Raghnaid nic Chaluim burned hers once with the hawk unhooded, and a clerk of the Hall came to question her. In FE 2,840 the eldest of the fowlers, Ealasaid Bhàn, turned the Hall's cutter away at her door and sent him home with the refusal set down on hide. It was the first rite to refuse the Hall's trial outright.

25.history: The river-folk of the Abhainn ìseal founded the town, and in the twenty-first century the dawn burning with the hawk spread up the river from Seann Skell to Inis ìseal and on to Cnoc bheag. The Keeper wrote that the rite kept the measure exactly and was no concern of the Hall's. It was the last time the Hall answered any rite so simply.

63.history: Hill-folk come down to the western shore founded the harbour. In FE 2,098 a merchant of Ros bheag, Aonghas Ruadh, came home from Baile àrsaidh with a boxed scorpion and swore his next bargain on its sting before the harbour court had seen it done. The court took up the oath for every trade, and from then on a merchant who would not swear on the sting was not trusted in the western harbours. Its merchants armed two boats against the raiders of the north-western waters, and seal-oil came down to its quays from Ceann mhòr for silver rings.
63.known_for: the sting-oath of the harbour court

246.history: Four miles south-east of Cnoc bhàn stood the millers' town where, in FE 2,300, Donnchadh mac Iain came with twenty-two hearers who had walked out of the stag's house. The reeve let them a millwright's storehouse for a rent paid that winter in mended roofs and re-hung doors, and ruled that their books keep no parentage. The school at Muileann chaol, the younger school of the stag, traded letters with the elders' school for the rest of the age. Donnchadh died here in FE 2,340. The oldest notched tallies of Ceann leathan's fish-market are kept here.

3.history: Farming kindreds founded the town on the south-eastern downs. In FE 2,386 a company of its men broke by night into the fallen walls of Làrach an Dùin on the strength of an old tale of riches and found only cold ash. The Keeper had them sentenced as though they had broken the Law, though no law covered it. Their families did penance by keeping the road from their town to Tuam Cnoc dhìreach in repair, and it is called the diggers' road still.

496.history: Carriers of the mountain country founded the halting-house below the pass. In the hungry season of FE 2,400 it carried more coal down than it was given grain back. When the late snow of FE 2,472 closed the passes, the common granaries were opened, and the reeves of Dùn dhearg sent grain up. The carrier Calum Ruadh and his son Iain Caol carried it up the pass, and Àth dhìreach granted the carriers the right to rest. The town extended the rest to whichever carrier of that road was oldest living, and the right died with Iain Caol, the last of the grain-carriers, in his ninetieth year.
496.known_for: the grain carried up in the poor season

493.history: Mountain households of the carriers' country founded Muileann gheal beside Àth dhìreach on the track to the pass. In the poor season of FE 2,472 it found, like its neighbours, that it had carried more than it was given back. The common granaries of the mountain were opened here on Oighrig nic Lachlainn's order, the first famine the rolls record as turned back.

255.history: The lords of the bent hill founded the town. In FE 2,578 the masons' fellowship bridged the river below it, joining the southern road to the western and saving a full day's cart-journey round through Cathair dhearg. The fellowship set the toll at half the capital's, holding it no fair thing to charge a full toll for half the road. The reeves of Cathair dhearg complained. The fellowship offered them the crossing, upkeep and all, and no reeve took the offer. The half-toll stood.

316.history: Oak-keepers of the capital's north founded the town on the southern road. Beathag Clachair was born here into a family of stone-cutters. At three-and-thirty she led the cutting of the small bridge over the stream that flooded every spring, and beneath the fourth hearth's sign in its keystone she cut her own name: Beathag Clachair a chuir seo. Within two seasons masons of every hearth were cutting their names beside the sign, and they call it Beathag's mark. She was buried at the foot of her bridge, and masons passing lay a chip of grey stone on her grave. Fearchar Ruadh, the mason's apprentice who won the stone field at Ceann leathan, came from Doire mhin.

95.history: Harbour-folk founded the town on the north-west coast. In the twenty-sixth century its fisher-families gathered under a headman of their own choosing and sent their tolls to Cathair dhearg only in the years a road-guard actually came so far to collect them. A reeve of Ros dhomhain wrote more than once that Caol mhòr paid what it pleased and answered to whom it pleased, and the red hall generally sent no answer.
95.known_for: the headman who answered to no reeve

143.history: Fishers founded the harbour on the north-west coast, and in the twenty-seventh century it found a trade the island came to depend on: seal-oil rendered from the seals of the northern rocks, carried down the western coast to Ros bheag for silver rings and burned in the beacons of every western harbour. The seal-oil lamps were the brightest light on Dia-thìr, and Ceann mhòr grew into a town of some standing on a coast where standing was hard come by.

489.history: The western Seann Skell, an old harbour of the Seann-Dhaoine, kept a harbour court whose oath had been sworn on a carved scorpion since before anyone could say why. In FE 2,846 the court's keepers made the oath a creed: one power alone stung the liar, Manannan mac Lir, lord of the sea, and the scorpion was his sign. From then on the oath was sworn over a cup marked with the scorpion. It was the first teaching on the island to claim that it alone was true.

94.history: The old harbour of the south-east coast below Cuan shean took up the sting-oath from its neighbour in FE 2,849 and carved its scorpion in yellow stone, the first image of the creature cut for worship. The stonecutter, better known for gravestones, carved it from a fisherman's telling of one washed up dead. On its fishing and on the silver of Muileann chiar, Seann Vell grew large enough to raise the first stone quay any harbour of the island built, and every southern harbour copied it.
94.known_for: the yellow scorpion and the first stone quay

297.history: Households of the south coast founded the town, and in the last years of the age families crowded out of the harbours about Cathair dhearg settled here and raised its long street along the ridge above the water. They brought a wood-watcher of their own rite and a copy of the laws, and the town grew.
297.known_for: the long street on the ridge

241.history: Red-earth farmers founded the town on the north-eastern coast. Near the end of the age a timber watch-tower went up here against raiders out of the islands, manned by turns by the fisher-kin of Sliochd Raghnaill. It was the only tower built for war in the whole Holy Age. Dòmhnall Dubh, whose kin kept it, married Mòr nic Coinnich, and when he died here in FE 2,950 she came north herself to bury him beside the tower.
